summary.text: Plasmodium is a genus of single-celled eukaryotes that are obligate parasites of vertebrates and of insects such as mosquitoes in the genus Anopheles.
A blood-feeding insect injects the parasites into a vertebrate during a blood meal, and they grow in body tissue, often the liver, before infecting red blood cells.
The destruction of host red blood cells can result in malaria, and parasites picked up by another blood-feeding insect continue the life cycle.

facts.label: First identified
facts.value: In the late 19th century by Charles Laveran

facts.label: Deadliest species
facts.value: P. falciparum, killing hundreds of thousands a year

facts.label: Genome
facts.value: Split into 14 chromosomes in the nucleus

items.prompt: A patient with malaria shares a home with her sister. Can the parasite pass between them through everyday contact?

options.label: Yes, through shared air
Yes, by touching infected skin
No, it cannot be spread from person to person
Only through shared food

items.explain: Plasmodium cannot be spread from person to person; it is introduced by an insect bite, and blood transfusion is very rare.

items.prompt: Plasmodium has just been injected by a mosquito bite. Where does it go first?

options.label: Liver or other tissue, replicating once before entering red blood cells
Straight into red blood cells, where it bursts them
The spleen, where it waits for symptoms
The brain, where it multiplies

items.explain: Parasites first infect the liver or other tissue and undergo a single large round of replication before exiting to infect erythrocytes.

items.prompt: Doctors keep developing new drugs against Plasmodium. What has the parasite done in response to each one?

options.label: Died out in the regions where it was used
Evolved resistance to it
Turned harmless to people
Moved to hosts that are not vertebrates

items.explain: A number of drugs have been developed, but the parasites have evolved resistance to each drug developed.

items.prompt: Some primate Plasmodium species can stay hidden in the liver for over a year. What is this dormant stage called?

options.label: Merozoite
Gametocyte
Apicoplast
Hypnozoite

items.explain: Some species of Plasmodium of primates can form a long-lived dormant stage called a hypnozoite, which can remain in the liver for more than a year.

items.prompt: A person infected with Plasmodium has no symptoms at all. Can the parasites still be multiplying inside them?

options.label: Yes, in large numbers hidden in places such as the spleen and bone marrow
No, no symptoms means the parasites have been cleared
Yes, but only inside the liver
Only if a mosquito bites them again

items.explain: Plasmodium infection can be asymptomatic, yet there can be very large numbers of multiplying parasites concealed in the spleen and bone marrow.

items.prompt: A Plasmodium cell is growing inside a red blood cell. Does it need its mitochondrion's ATP-making function there?

options.label: Yes, it is the parasite's only energy source in red cells
Yes, since red blood cells lack energy to share
No, that function is only needed to survive in the insect host
No, because Plasmodium has no mitochondrion

items.explain: The mitochondrion can generate ATP, but this function is only required for survival in the insect host and not for growth in red blood cells.

paragraphs.heading: A parasite with two hosts
paragraphs.text: Plasmodium is a genus of single-celled eukaryotes that must live as parasites, in vertebrates and in insects such as Anopheles mosquitoes. A blood-feeding insect injects the parasites into a vertebrate as it feeds. They grow in a body tissue, often the liver, then move into the bloodstream and infect red blood cells. Destroying those cells can cause malaria, and when another insect feeds, it picks up some parasites and the cycle goes on.

paragraphs.heading: Many species, many hosts
paragraphs.text: More than 200 species of Plasmodium have been described. They are found around the world wherever suitable hosts live. Their vertebrate hosts include reptiles, birds and mammals, and their insect hosts are most often mosquitoes of the genera Culex and Anopheles. Plasmodium belongs to the Apicomplexa, a large group of parasitic eukaryotes.

paragraphs.heading: Plasmodium and people
paragraphs.text: Charles Laveran first identified these parasites in the late 19th century. Five species regularly infect humans. They are Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium malariae, Plasmodium ovale and Plasmodium knowlesi. Of these, Plasmodium falciparum is by far the deadliest, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths a year. Drugs have been developed to treat the infection, but the parasites have evolved resistance to each one. Infection through a blood transfusion is possible but very rare, and the parasite cannot spread from one person to another.

paragraphs.heading: Tools for breaking in
paragraphs.text: Like its relatives, Plasmodium has special organelles at its apical end for releasing substances into the host. The most prominent are the bulb-shaped rhoptries, holding proteins used to invade a host cell and to change it once inside. Next to them sit smaller micronemes, with proteins for moving and for recognising and gripping host cells. Dense granules spread through the cell carry proteins that modify the parasitophorous vacuole, the membrane between parasite and host.

paragraphs.heading: Two borrowed organelles
paragraphs.text: Plasmodium also has two large organelles of endosymbiotic origin: a mitochondrion and the apicoplast. Mammal cells have many mitochondria, but a Plasmodium cell has just one large one, which divides in step with the cell. It can make energy as ATP through the citric acid cycle, yet the parasite needs this only inside the insect, not while growing in red blood cells. The apicoplast came from a red alga taken in by an ancestor of Plasmodium. It helps make fatty acids, isoprenoids, iron-sulphur clusters and parts of the heme pathway.

paragraphs.heading: Hiding in the body
paragraphs.text: In the vertebrate, the parasites first infect the liver or another tissue and multiply in one large round before leaving to infect red blood cells. At this point some species that infect primates can form a hypnozoite, a dormant stage that can stay in the liver for more than a year. In the blood they cycle through red cells again and again, while a few turn into gametocytes, the sexual stage that a feeding insect takes up. In some hosts infection seems to cause no symptoms, yet even in such human infections huge numbers of parasites can be hidden, especially in the spleen and bone marrow.
